title: ControlG: Feedback Control for Multi-Objective Graph Learning
one_liner: Instead of forcing every weight update to compromise between competing goals, a control-theory scheduler decides WHEN each goal gets to train, preventing conflicts and starvation.
lead: When you teach a graph model to do multiple tasks at once—finding mutual similarities, reconstructing data, and contrasting examples—they often fight for the same weights. The usual approach weights them per update, but that leaves some tasks starved while others dominate. ControlG recasts this as a scheduling problem: measure how hard each task is to learn and when tasks clash, let a control system decide when each one should get optimization time, producing an auditable schedule that reveals which tasks actually drove learning.

problem.h2: The tug-of-war between competing graph objectives
paras: Graph models learn from unlabeled data by inventing their own training tasks. One task might say: find pairs of examples that are similar. Another says: rebuild the input from a noisy version. A third says: examples that should be close end up far apart, and far ones stay far. Each task pulls the weights in a different direction.

The naive approach: on every weight update, take a weighted average of the three task nudges and move the weights by that average. But this creates three hidden problems. First, Disagreement: if task A wants weights to move up and task B wants them down, the average nudge is small, so neither task makes much progress—learning one task actually weakens the other. Second, Drift: as training proceeds, some tasks become easier while others get harder, yet a fixed average weight stays unchanged, missing this shift. Third, Drought: if tasks have mismatched difficulties, a uniform weight starves the hard tasks—because the average nudge is tiny compared to the signal they need, they never climb out of noise.

callout.html: The paper recasts multi-objective learning as a scheduling problem: measure each task's difficulty and conflict with others, then use a control system to decide when each task should receive optimization budget.

steps.text: Estimate how hard each objective is to optimize by watching how much its loss shrinks per training step.
For each pair of tasks, compute how much one task's nudge opposes the other's on the same weights.
Use a Pareto-optimal planner to decide what fraction of training time each task should get, trading off between all objectives fairly.
A PID controller (a standard tool from engineering) adjusts the schedule in real time if any task falls behind or gets too much focus.
The final schedule shows which task to train on each step, revealing the real learning path.

object.h2: What the paper changes: the allocation schedule
paras: Instead of a fixed weight per objective, the paper introduces a time-varying schedule that decides which single objective receives the full optimization budget at each training step. Rather than blending all the nudges together into one weak average, you apply one task's nudge fully, then switch to another task's nudge, then another, rotating based on measured difficulty and conflict.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: pairwise task antagonism
hidden.name: task antagonism (how much one task's nudge opposes another's)
paras: Task antagonism is a single number (or a matrix) that measures how much two objectives conflict on shared weights. If task A's nudge says move a weight up and task B's nudge says move it down, antagonism is high. If both nudges point in the same direction, antagonism is low. Antagonism is hidden because you do not see it directly—only when tasks interfere with each other in training.

The paper estimates antagonism by computing the dot product of gradient vectors between pairs of tasks. Positive dot products mean they agree (low antagonism); negative or near-zero dot products mean they fight (high antagonism). High antagonism tasks should rarely run together; the scheduler will give them separate time slots to avoid cancellation.

heat.caption: Darker cells show high conflict between tasks, high difficulty, or high allocated time.

reads.html: Task antagonism is the amount two learning goals block each other. High antagonism means they want opposite moves; the scheduler pulls them apart in time to stop them cancelling.

The paper estimates antagonism by computing the dot product of the nudges each task wants to make (its gradients on the shared weights). Positive means they agree; negative means they fight. This measurement feeds into the Pareto-aware log-hypervolume planner.

paras: Static weighting forces every weight update to be a compromise. For example, pulling 40% toward task A, 30% toward B, and 30% toward C. If task A and B want opposite moves, their contributions cancel and both make no progress—the weights barely shift. Scheduling instead flips the logic: run task A alone for several steps, letting its full force push the weights without opposition. Then switch to task B's turn. Since each task acts in isolation (or with friendly partners), the weights move decisively instead of getting stuck.

Why this works: A gradient pointing uphill has force. When two opposing forces meet, they neutralize each other. But if you apply force A fully, then force B fully, then force C fully, each one pushes the weights without resistance, and they end up further along than if you applied weak versions of all three at once. The scheduler ensures this by measuring which tasks fight (high antagonism) and keeping them in separate time slots.

The PID controller tightens the loop: measure how much each task has improved since its last turn. If task B is falling behind, give it the next turn. If task C just improved a lot, reduce its next allocation. This prevents starvation (the hard tasks get more turns) and prevents nonstationary problems (the scheduler continuously re-measures as difficulty changes). The auditable schedule itself proves what learning path the model took.

stages.s: Three task nudges and last schedule
Measure how hard each task is and how much they conflict
Plan fair time split across all tasks using Pareto frontier
Control loop adjusts schedule based on recent task progress
Next task to train at full force

math.h2: The core equation: antagonism and Pareto planning
math.words: antagonism(A,B) = sum over shared weights of gradient_A times gradient_B, divided by their lengths; target_allocation solves: maximize log(product of per-task final accuracies) subject to total training budget and pairwise antagonism constraints.
math.equation: antagonism(i,j) = dot(grad_i, grad_j) / (norm(grad_i) * norm(grad_j)); allocate_t = argmax sum_i log(acc_i_target) s.t. sum_t allocate_t = T, antagonism(i, j) < threshold if overlap(t_i, t_j) > 0
symbols: the nudge direction task i wants for shared weights
the magnitude or length of a gradient vector
how aligned the two gradients are (positive if same direction)
expected accuracy for task i under the proposed schedule
binary choice: does task i get training time at step t
maximum antagonism allowed if two tasks train in the same window

charts.title: Static weighting (naive average)
charts.note: All tasks suffer because nudges in opposite directions cancel each other out. No objective gets enough force to improve much past random guessing, because its signal is always drowned out by the average of the others.

charts.title: ControlG scheduling
charts.note: Each task gets dedicated training time. Full nudges act without opposition. Accuracies for all three tasks climb together because each one's signal is no longer diluted by the other two.

items.b: Antagonism estimation is noisy early in training.
items.html: If you measure conflict too early, the task gradients are unstable, giving false antagonism scores. The schedule might keep misaligned tasks apart when they actually agree. Workaround: warm up the antagonism estimates over the first few epochs, or smooth them with a moving average.

If the controller reacts too aggressively to a task falling behind, it might allocate far too much time to it next, causing other tasks to starve in the opposite direction. Requires tuning the controller gains (proportional, integral, derivative terms) per dataset.

The log-hypervolume planner might heavily favor one task over others. At the Pareto frontier, any improvement to one task requires sacrificing another. Some plans might leave one task neglected if what you value differs from the planner's fairness model. May need manual constraint tightening to enforce minimum allocations.

items.b: Done right, antagonism guides the schedule.
items.html: When antagonism is estimated cleanly and the PID gains are tuned, the schedule naturally separates conflicting tasks and gives dedicated time to starved ones, eliminating the hidden interference.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a graph dataset with three clear objectives: mutual information (maximize similarity between augmented views), reconstruction (predict missing nodes), and contrastive (push apart dissimilar examples). Train a graph neural network using three methods: (1) static 1/3 weight to each, (2) per-update adaptive weighting based on loss magnitudes, and (3) ControlG's schedule. Log the antagonism matrix at each epoch and the schedule decisions (which task trained when). Track individual task accuracy throughout training, not just end performance.
demo.metric_eq: improvement_per_task = (ControlG_final_acc_i - static_weighting_final_acc_i) for each task i; schedule_utilization = number of steps each task was scheduled; interference_score = mean(antagonism) for task pairs scheduled in the same window
demo.closing: The demo makes clear that scheduling prevents cancellation. Watch all three task accuracies climb together because the schedule separates conflicting tasks into different time windows, letting each full nudge act without opposition, unlike the average where they dilute each other.
